newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - Budapest bourse soars but small size hurts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Budapest bourse soars but small size hurts.

text.p: The soaring Budapest Stock Exchange hit another record high on Wednesday but is being hampered by its small size and failure to attract enough new listings, analysts said.
"A little bit of money goes a long way in Hungary because the market is very small," said James Oates, director for central and eastern Europe at UBS in London.
"The market capitalisation is less than $7.5 billion and in western Europe one company would be $100 billion," said Spencer Jakab, analyst at CSFB in Budapest. "It is still really small."
"Therefore it has to get to the size of at least 30 percent of GDP so in the long run Hungarian companies that are very promising will want to list themselves on the market."
Budapest has been one of the fastest growing emerging markets last year and this, and the BUX index hit a record close of 6,779.59 points on Wednesday.
Listings include companies with 30 to 40 percent annual growth potential and the index is supported by an economy which is growing strongly following austerity in 1995.

Economists believe Hungary is an increasingly safe place to invest. They cite the country's membership of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) since March 1996, its investment grade rating by the leading international credit agencies and its prospects for NATO membership.

"Hungary's overall risk profile for equity investors would now compare favourably with many western European countries and is clearly ahead of most central and eastern European peers," Daiwa Europe Ltd said in its June "Equity Strategy Quarterly".
But market participants say the bourse might fall in the longer term as its importance in central Europe turns around.

"In the medium term Hungary is going to remain a core portfolio within the eastern European emerging markets portfolio," said Rudi Voros, analyst at ICE Securities in London. "(But) the whole region is changing, sooner or later other markets will be interesting as well."
Romania is already an interesting market, Croatia is becoming one again and Serbia is expected to open in about half a year while Ukraine is a little bit further off, Voros added.
Most market participants say that investors want more opportunities than the 47 issues traded on the Hungarian bourse, but some analysts say small is good.
"In the Czech Republic there are some 2,000 companies registered on the bourse, but of these 2,000 only 10 to 15 trade actively," Voros said.

"Formally the Czech market has a huge capitalisation, but this is worth nothing as the Hungarian market is much more liquid than the Czech and there are days when it is more liquid than the Polish market."

Budapest's equity market capitalisation has risen to 1.3 trillion forints ($7 billion) by the end of May 1997, from 852.5 billion at the end of 1996 and 327.8 billion at the end of 1995, according to BSE figures.
The May capitalisation was around 20 percent of Hungary's GDP but this is below the emerging market average of around 30 percent and certain sectors are mostly or even totally absent.

Market participants expect liquidity to improve with the listing of electricity and gas distributors, and some other major companies such as commercial vehicle maker Raba, plus shares of the national air carrier Malev and in the telecommunications giant Matav. But listings do not depend on privatisation agency APV alone.

Gyorgy Pinke, head of APV's Capital Market and Property Transfer Managing Directorate, said earlier this month that APV was committed to encouraging the listing of the six electricity distributors but said that under Hungary's securities act the companies themselves had to initiate the listing.
OTP Bank and oil and gas company MOL Rt, which are already listed, could boost liquidity with the government pledging to sell all but one golden share in each.
Analysts see the bourse's role changing in the coming years but also say long-term globalisation of markets will decrease its importance.
"It is becoming a much more attractive option for raising money because the banks in Hungary only want to lend to the blue chips," said CSFB's Jakab.
"I guess it's going to be something like the Portuguese or Danish exchange in 10 years' time," he said. "It's going to exist but it's not going to be one of the major markets."
